ca_sonora_pass_highway_108.blurb: Highway 108 climbing is a string of separate crags rather than one cliff, running from the San Joaquin Valley foothills near Sonora east toward the Sierra Nevada crest. Sport, trad and bouldering each make up roughly a third of the climbs, with a little top-rope and ice. Roped grades run from easy to 5.14, with the biggest cluster at 5.10 and plenty more through 5.11 to 5.13, while problems range from easy up to V10. Table Mountain is a long, flat-topped ridge of latite with sheer trad and sport walls, and fall is an especially good time for it. Jailhouse Rock is mostly sport, Columbia Bouldering holds the largest number of problems, and Upper Highway 108 and Chipmunk Flat add smaller crags.

ca_wonderland_of_rocks.blurb: A maze of granite domes and boulder piles inside Joshua Tree National Park, the Wonderland is big, complicated terrain where it is easy to lose your bearings. It splits into a northern and a southern half, with the north holding the larger number of climbs. Traditional climbing dominates by a wide margin, mostly crack and face lines, with a smaller share of sport, top-rope and a few boulder problems. Some routes are multi-pitch. Grades run from easy to the low 5.13s, but most sit between 5.8 and 5.11, with 5.10 the most common. Expect a quieter, more remote feel than the roadside formations elsewhere in the park, since reaching the rock means a real walk in.

bc_castlegar.blurb: Castlegar sits where the Columbia and Kootenay rivers meet in the West Kootenay, and its cliffs are close to town. Climbing here goes back to the 1950s. Bouldering is the biggest share of the climbing, followed by sport and then trad, with a few top-ropes. Roped routes mostly fall between 5.8 and 5.12 with 5.10 the most common grade, and problems are mostly V0 to V6 with a few harder ones. Arrow Lake has the greatest number of climbs, Kinnaird Bluffs is the long-established mix of sport and trad for all levels, and Waterline adds more cragging. Walls facing south dry out early, and can be climbed as soon as February, while fully sunny faces suit spring and fall better than summer afternoons.

ct_central_valley.blurb: Central Connecticut's climbing is on traprock, the volcanic basalt that forms the long ridgelines through the middle of the state. Ragged Mountain, on the Metacomet Ridge west of New Britain, is the best known; its cliffs come from tilted lava flows laid down long ago. Trad is the main event, with a sizable bouldering scene, some top-rope and a little sport. Grades run from easy up to 5.12 or so, with most climbs between 5.7 and 5.11, so moderates are well served. Pinnacle Rock, Rattlesnake Mountain and Bradley Mountain are other big clusters, and the cliffs are spread over a number of separate ridges rather than gathered in one place.

id_central_idaho.blurb: This region covers the mountains and valleys around Sun Valley and Ketchum, Stanley, Challis and Salmon, so the climbing is scattered across several ranges. Sport is the largest share, much of it at The Fins on the southern end of the Lost River Range, a limestone area of vertical to slightly overhanging walls with edges and pockets. Most of its sport lines run from about 5.10 to 5.13. Walls there get morning sun and are mostly shaded by early afternoon, which makes hot summer afternoons workable. The Sawtooth Range brings multi-pitch trad and alpine climbing, and bouldering is concentrated around Rock Creek, Redfish Lake and Salmon. Roped grades are centered on 5.10 to 5.12.

bc_the_smoke_bluffs.blurb: The Smoke Bluffs is a cluster of small granite crags on a forested hill just across the highway from downtown Squamish. Approaches are short, and most routes are a single pitch, with a few longer ones. Traditional climbing is by far the main style, with a smaller amount of sport and a little bouldering. The granite offers pure cracks, friction slabs and delicate faces, mostly vertical to slabby with a few overhangs. Grades run from easy 5.4s through 5.13, with 5.10 the most common and a strong supply of 5.7 to 5.9 for moderate leaders. Burgers and Fries and Crag X are among its larger walls, though the climbing is spread over dozens of separate crags.
